tier_reason: First-party db_bench comparison against SQLite 3.39.5. The benchmark code is public (andy-byers/leveldb, branch db_bench_calicodb, benchmarks/db_bench_calicodb.cc and benchmarks/db_bench_sqlite3.cc), but the page states only 'compiled with gcc', with no version or flags, and the runs are on generic GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest and macos-latest runners with no CPU model. That falls short of A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Latency in microseconds per op, CalicoDB 0.0.1 vs SQLite3 3.39.5. readrand100K: 58.801 vs 252.367 on Linux (~4.3x, derived from page data) and 79.160 vs 495.537 on macOS (~6.3x, derived). readseq100K: 58.518 vs 89.065 on Linux (~1.5x, derived) and 74.773 vs 203.458 on macOS (~2.7x, derived). fillseqbatch: 1.040 vs 2.033 on Linux (~2.0x, derived). fillseq: 23.056 vs 29.767 on Linux (~1.3x, derived). Results are mixed. On Linux CalicoDB is slower on fillrandom, fillrandbatch, overwrite, overwritebatch, readrandom (4.613 vs 4.270) and fillrand100K. On macOS it is slower on fillrandom, fillrandbatch, overwrite and overwritebatch, and much slower on fillseqsync (1101.377 vs 291.237, ~3.8x slower) and fillrandsync (1117.884 vs 213.655, ~5.2x slower) because it uses F_FULLFSYNC.
corrections.workload: LevelDB db_bench adapted to CalicoDB and SQLite (fillseq, fillseqsync, fillseqbatch, fillrandom, fillrandsync, fillrandbatch, overwrite, overwritebatch, readrandom, readseq, fillrand100K, fillseq100K, readseq100K, readrand100K), run in CI on GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest and macos-latest. CalicoDB 0.0.1 (commit 30fe767) vs SQLite3 3.39.5. SQLite was configured with a WITHOUT ROWID table, WAL mode, 4 KiB pages, synchronous=NORMAL (FULL for the *sync benchmarks) and EXCLUSIVE locking.
corrections.caveats: Benchmarked on generic CI runners with no CPU model and no stated compiler version or flags, so it falls short of Tier A despite public benchmark code. The author's disclaimer says SQLite is an RDBMS with more per-operation overhead than a KV store, and the README says CalicoDB is 'not ready for production'. The results are for an old commit (30fe767). Wins are concentrated in large-value (100K) reads and sequential or batched fills; CalicoDB is slower on random and overwrite writes, and several times slower on the macOS *sync benchmarks. No commits since November 2023.

notes: The page numbers match the record exactly. The original claimed_speedup undercounted where CalicoDB loses: readrandom on Linux, overwritebatch, fillrand100K on Linux, and the macOS *sync benchmarks. The last commit (2023-11-01) makes it stale; 43 stars and the MIT license are verified.

tier_reason: A first-party live CI dashboard against RocksDB v8.10.2 and RocksDB master. The code is public (.github/workflows/db_bench-build.yml, db_bench-run.yml, .github/scripts/build_upstream_rocksdb.sh, .github/bench-conf) and the page states the CPU model (AMD EPYC 7763, 4 vCPU). The workflow shows release builds (DEBUG_LEVEL=0, PORTABLE=haswell), but neither the page nor the run states which compiler or version was used; a use_clang input switches between gcc and clang. So not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Run of 2026-09-15 (run_id 34935695406), fillrandom suite, readrandom stage. ToplingDB zipkeyvalue reached 1,735,572 ops/sec vs 348,705 for RocksDB v8.10 (4.98x, stated on the page, which calls this 'the fairest comparison') and vs 378,878 for RocksDB master (4.58x, on page). ToplingDB zipkeyonly, which stores values uncompressed while RocksDB uses Snappy/Zstd, reached 4,720,755 ops/sec: 13.54x vs v8.10 and 12.46x vs master (on page). Other stages: fillrandom 1,660,002 vs 664,354 ops/sec (2.50x, on page) and readseq 16,936,378 vs 10,771,647 (1.57x, on page). ToplingDB is slower on compaction: zipkeyvalue runs at 0.62x of v8.10 in the fillrandom suite and 0.30x in the fillseq suite. The page is a live dashboard, so the numbers change with each CI run.
corrections.workload: db_bench fillrandom, fillseq and fillseq (CSPP) suites (fill, flush, compact, readseq x3, readrandom): 50,000,000 records, 8-byte keys, 50-byte values, batch_size 1000. The DB lives on /dev/shm (tmpfs) and the on-disk DB (~1.9 GiB for fillrandom) fits inside the 7.8 GiB RocksDB block cache. ToplingDB uses ToplingZipTable (zipkeyonly/zipkeyvalue), the CSPP memtable and -enable_zero_copy.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated on the page. The public CI workflow builds ToplingDB with `make ... DEBUG_LEVEL=0` and upstream RocksDB with DEBUG_LEVEL=0 PORTABLE=haswell (to match ToplingDB's -march=haswell). The compiler is the ubuntu-latest default (gcc) unless the workflow's use_clang input is set, and the version is unstated.
corrections.hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 64-Core Processor (4 logical CPUs; GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runner, Azure kernel 6.17), Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS, 15.6 GiB RAM, DB on /dev/shm
corrections.caveats: The benchmark is run and published by the ToplingDB project itself, and the results page does not name the compiler. The dataset sits entirely in cache on tmpfs, which the page itself calls a CPU/memory comparison, so the result may not carry over to larger-than-cache workloads. The 13.5x headline uses zipkeyonly, which leaves values uncompressed against a compressed RocksDB and uses 1.24-1.97x more disk; the fair zipkeyvalue figure is ~5x. Compaction is slower than RocksDB. Most importantly, the components benchmarked, the ToplingZipTable builder (private topling-rocks repo) and the CSPP MemTable (private), are closed source; the build downloads them as precompiled 90-day trial objects. Only the RocksDB-derived core and some plugins are open (GPL-2.0/Apache-2.0 inherited from RocksDB).

notes: The numbers match the 2026-09-15 run. The record's 'RocksDB master 378,000' should read 378,878, and the 13.5x ratio is printed on the page, not just derived. ToplingDB is a RocksDB fork (the README says 'forked from RocksDB', and db_bench reports version 8.10.2), even though GitHub's fork flag is false. The key performance components are proprietary trial binaries, hence usability 'mixed'.

tier_reason: A first-party table ('As of December 2022, typical results can look like') comparing UDisk with RocksDB, with no hardware, compiler, flags or dataset size given for the table. The harness (unum-cloud/ucsb) is public, but the engine under test (UDisk) is a closed-source binary, so the result cannot be reproduced.

corrections.claimed_speedup: As of December 2022 (first-party table, ops/sec, RocksDB -> UDisk): Batch Read 650K -> 4.5M (~6.9x, derived from page data); Batch Upsert 57K -> 260K (~4.6x, derived); Read 420K -> 1M (~2.4x, derived); Read & Update 1:1 64K -> 173K (~2.7x, derived); Read & Upsert 19:1 128K -> 270K (~2.1x, derived); Remove 420K -> 874K (~2.1x, derived); Scan 17M vs 17M (no gain).
corrections.workload: Binary KV operations (scan, batch read, read, read & update 1:1, read & upsert 19:1, batch upsert, remove) via the UCSB harness, UDisk vs RocksDB. The table does not give the collection size; the page links separate UCSB result posts for 1 TB and 10 TB collections.
corrections.caveats: The benchmarked engine, UDisk, is closed source. UStore's own engines table marks it Open-Source ✗, UStore's CMake only links a prebuilt UDisk static library through USTORE_ENGINE_UDISK_PATH, and the unum-cloud/UDisk repo holds only a README, docs and assets. The Apache-2.0 UStore repo covers the bindings plus the UCSet, LevelDB and RocksDB adapters, not the engine being measured. The table is labeled 'typical results ... as of December 2022', with no hardware, compiler or dataset size; the UCSB harness repo has no LICENSE file. The default branch (main, the only branch) was last committed 2023-08-18 even though the repo's pushed_at is 2026-09-15.

notes: The table numbers match the record. '1 TB' is not stated for this table, and the old caveat about 'more recent pushes to other branches' is wrong, since main is the only branch. The measured engine UDisk is proprietary and binary-only, so the orchestrator may want to retag or rename the entry: nothing benchmarked here can be copied.
